## Chapter VI

ROME (1859-1860)

The tramp in Thüringen lasted four-and-twenty hours. By the end of the first walk, his three companions—all Boston and Harvard like himself—were satisfied; when they sat down to rest on the spot where Goethe had written—

"Warte nur! balde Rubest du auch!"—

the wisdom of the advice affected them so strongly that they hired a wagon and drove to Weimar the same night. None could say why they had come to Germany, or why they stayed. Adams stayed because he did not want to go home.

A few days at Dresden satisfied them that Dresden was a better spot for general education than Berlin, and equally good for reading Civil Law. There was nothing to study there, but the Sistine Madonna and the Correggios were famous, the theatre excellent, and the Elbe prettier than the Spree. He took a room in the household of a small government clerk and continued the language. Possibly one might learn something more by accident, as one had learned something of Beethoven. For the next eighteen months the young man pursued accidental education, since he could pursue no other.

Perhaps the chief obstacle to his education was his honesty—his simple-minded faith in his intentions. He still persuaded himself that his German education was a success. The Germany he loved was the eighteenth-century Germany the Germans were ashamed of, and were destroying as fast as they could. Military Germany was his abhorrence. What he liked was the simple character, the good-natured sentiment, the musical and metaphysical abstraction, the blundering incapacity of the German for practical affairs. Until coal-power and railways were created she was mediæval by nature and geography, and this was what Adams, under the teachings of Carlyle and Lowell, liked.

He was floundering between worlds passed and worlds coming. Suddenly the Emperor Napoleon declared war on Austria and raised a confused point of morals in the mind of Europe. France was the wicked spirit of moral politics, and whatever helped France must be evil. Austria was another evil spirit. Italy was the prize. Should one be Guelph or Ghibelline? Wisdom had been singularly baffled by the problem. Better take sides first, and reason about it for the rest of life.

Luckily he had a sister much brighter than he ever was, who after marrying Charles Kuhn had come to Italy and, like all good Americans, was hotly Italian. In July, 1859, she was at Thun, and there Henry joined her. She adored Italy and disliked Germany. She was the first young woman he was ever intimate with—quick, sensitive, wilful, energetic, sympathetic and intelligent enough to supply a score of men with ideas—and he was delighted to give her the reins. In after life he made a general law of experience: no woman had ever driven him wrong; no man had ever driven him right.

Nothing would satisfy her but to go to the seat of war. The party crossed the St. Gothard and reached Milan. To young Adams this first plunge into Italy passed Beethoven as a piece of accidental education—not a means of pursuing life but one of the ends attained. Not satisfied with Milan, she insisted on invading the enemy's country by the Stelvio Pass. Where the glacier of the Ortler Spitze tumbled its huge mass down upon the road, the carriage was stopped by the double line of sentries stretching up the mountains till the flash of the gun barrels was lost in the flash of the snow. The eternal woman, when she is young, pretty, and engaging, had her way; in fifteen minutes the carriage was rolling down to Mals.

He went back to Dresden, faithful to his scheme of two winters in the Civil Law. There were no accidents in Dresden. As soon as the winter was over he closed and locked the German door, and took the road to Italy. In spite of the infinite variety of new impressions he knew no more, for his practical purposes, than the day he graduated. Nothing had been further from his mind in November, 1858, than to become a tourist; but a mere tourist, and nothing else, he had become in April, 1860, when he joined his sister in Florence. Supposing his father asked him on his return what equivalent he had brought back—the only possible answer would be: "Sir, I am a tourist!"

Meanwhile his father had perplexities of his own. His Quincy district had sent him to Congress, and in the spring of 1860 he was nominating candidates, supporting Mr. Seward. The Republican Party was an unknown force; the Democratic torn to pieces. For the time, the young man was safe from interference, and went on his way with a light heart.

Perhaps the most useful purpose he set himself was his pen: long letters to his brother Charles, printed in the Boston Courier. He had little to say, and said it not very well, but the habit of expression leads to the search for something to express.

Italy was mostly an emotion, and the emotion centred in Rome. Rome before 1870 was seductive beyond resistance. The lights and shadows were still mediæval, and mediæval Rome was alive; the shadows breathed and glowed. No sand-blast of science had yet skinned off the epidermis of history, thought, and feeling. The pictures were uncleaned, the churches unrestored, the ruins unexcavated. Rome was the worst spot on earth to teach nineteenth-century youth what to do with a twentieth-century world; yet it was the only spot the young of every race passionately, perversely, wickedly loved.

To a young Bostonian, fresh from Germany, Rome seemed a pure emotion; yet it was piling up conundrum after conundrum that seemed unconnected but he had got to connect, insoluble but had got to be somehow solved. Rome was actual; it was England; it was going to be America. Rome could not be fitted into an orderly, middle-class, Bostonian scheme of evolution. No law of progress applied to it. Not even time-sequences—the last refuge of helpless historians—had value for it. The Forum no more led to the Vatican than the Vatican to the Forum. The great word Evolution had not yet, in 1860, made a new religion of history, but the old religion had preached the same doctrine for a thousand years without finding in the entire history of Rome anything but flat contradiction.

More than once Adams sat at sunset on the steps of the Church of Santa Maria di Ara Cœli, wondering that not an inch had been gained by Gibbon—or all the historians since—towards explaining the Fall. None of them could say more than the tourist who went on repeating to himself the eternal question—Why! Why!! Why!!!—as his neighbor, the blind beggar, might do, sitting next him on the church steps. Substitute the word America for the word Rome, and the question became personal.

He went on to Naples, and there in the hot June heard rumors that Garibaldi was about to attack Palermo. The American Minister sent him as bearer of despatches; he found Garibaldi at supper in the Senate House towards sunset, in the noise and color of the revolution. Garibaldi sat down at the window for a few words of talk. In the summer of 1860 he was the most serious of the doubtful energies in the world. Adams had the chance to look this sphinx in the eyes for five minutes, and to watch him like a wild animal. One saw a quiet-featured, quiet-voiced man in a red flannel shirt; absolutely impervious; a type of which Adams knew nothing. Sympathetic it was; one felt that it was simple; one suspected even that it might be childlike, but could form no guess of its intelligence. In his own eyes Garibaldi might be a Napoleon or Spartacus; in the hands of Cavour, a Condottiere; in the eyes of history, only the vigorous player in the game he did not understand. The lesson of Garibaldi seemed to teach the extreme complexity of extreme simplicity.

He came north to squander two or three months on Paris, which he had always avoided. He disapproved of France in the lump—the Empire, the Emperor, most of all the French mind. Yet, being in no way responsible for the French, he felt quite at liberty to enjoy everything he disapproved. He acquired a modest taste for Bordeaux and Burgundy, for the Palais Royal Theatre and the rest. He studied nothing, entered no society, made no acquaintance. After staying as long as he could, he started with mixed emotions but no education for home.

## Chapter VII

TREASON (1860-1861)

When forty years afterwards Henry Adams looked back, he asked whether fortune had ever dealt its cards quite so wildly as when it led him to begin the study of law and to vote for Abraham Lincoln on the same day.

He dropped back on Quincy like a lump of lead; he rebounded like a football, tossed into space by an unknown energy which played with all his generation as a cat plays with mice. Not one man in America wanted the Civil War, or expected or intended it. The vast majority wanted to go on with their occupations in peace. Not one, however clever, guessed what happened.

The prodigal was welcomed home; even his father asked no malicious question about the Pandects, but quietly invited his son to act as private secretary during the winter in Washington. Although no one believed in civil war, the air reeked of it, and the Republicans organized their Wide-Awakes in a form military in all things except weapons. Henry reached home in time to see the last of these processions file down through the November night to the Old House, where Mr. Adams, their Member of Congress, received them; their air was not that of innocence.

Profoundly ignorant, anxious, and curious, he packed his trunk again and started for Washington. Ten years had passed since his last visit, but very little had changed. The same rude colony was camped in the same forest, with the same unfinished Greek temples for work rooms and sloughs for roads. The Government had an air of social instability that went far to support the right of secession in theory as in fact.

Of all the crowd swarming in Washington that winter, young Adams was surely among the most ignorant and helpless, but he saw that the knowledge possessed by everybody about him was hardly greater than his own. The Southern secessionists were certainly unbalanced—haunted by suspicion, by idèes fixes, by violent morbid excitement. The cotton-planters were mentally one-sided and provincial to a degree rarely known. They showed a young student his first object-lesson of the way in which excess of power worked when held by inadequate hands. From the Confederate school, no one learned a useful lesson except to keep away.

Perforce, the student was thrown back on Northern precept. The New England type was one's self; it had nothing to show except one's own features. Setting aside Sumner, all the New Englanders were sane and steady men, but the New Englander's strength was his poise, which almost amounted to a defect. The character was familiar; one knew it to the core; one was it.

The hope of education narrowed itself to two men—Sumner and Seward.

Sumner, fifty years old, had passed beyond the reach of his boy friend; eight or ten years of solitary existence as Senator had developed in him the dogmatism of all the dogmatic stations. Yet he had at least the merit of qualities that warranted dogmatism. He justly thought that his services, his oratorical power, his political experience, his representative character at the head of the New England contingent, made him the most important member of the Senate.

Senator Seward was an old friend of the family, who professed to be a disciple of John Quincy Adams. A few days after the Adamses arrived in December, 1860, the Governor came to dinner alone. A slouching, slender figure; a head like a wise macaw; a beaked nose; shaggy eyebrows; unorderly hair and clothes; hoarse voice; offhand manner; free talk, and perpetual cigar—offered a new type to fathom. Seward was never petty or personal; his talk was large; he had some means, unknown to other Senators, of producing the effect of unselfishness. From the first sight, Henry loved the Governor.

The President-elect had selected Seward for Secretary of State. The new Administration decided that, before they could administer the Government, they must make sure of a government to administer, and that this chance depended on the action of Virginia. Seward took the lead in the Senate; Mr. Adams in the House; in offering concessions to the border States they ran the risk of dividing their own party. As Seward himself, in his gruff way, said at dinner: "If there's no secession now, you and I are ruined."

He saw Mr. Lincoln but once; at the melancholy function called an Inaugural Ball. He saw a long, awkward figure; a plain, ploughed face; a mind, absent in part, and in part evidently worried by white kid gloves; features that expressed neither self-satisfaction nor any other familiar Americanism, but rather the same painful sense of becoming educated and of needing education that tormented a private secretary; above all a lack of apparent force.

Henry recognized at the same moment, in another young man named John Hay, a friend; never lost sight of him at the future crossing of their paths. Friends are born, not made; he never mistook a friend except when in power.

He was thunderstruck to learn that Senator Sumner privately denounced the family's course, regarded Mr. Adams as betraying the principles of his life, and broke off relations. He cared little or nothing about the point in discussion; he liked lofty moral principle and cared little for political tactics; he felt a profound respect for Sumner; but the shock opened a chasm in life that never closed, and as long as life lasted, he found himself invariably taking for granted, as a political instinct—as he took for granted that arsenic poisoned—the rule that a friend in power is a friend lost.

This was the result of the new attempt at education. Washington was a dismal school. Lincoln, Seward, Sumner, and the rest could give no help; they knew less than he; within six weeks they were all to be taught their duties by the uprising of such as he, and their education was to cost a million lives. With the close of the session, his own functions ended. He returned to Boston in the middle of March and, with childlike docility, sat down at a desk in the law-office of Horace Gray to begin again: "My Lords and Gentlemen."

## Chapter VIII

DIPLOMACY (1861)

Hardly a week passed when the newspapers announced that President Lincoln had selected Charles Francis Adams as his Minister to England. Once more, silently, Henry put Blackstone back on its shelf. Mr. Adams once more intimated that he thought himself entitled to the services of one of his sons, and indicated Henry as the only one who could be spared from more serious duties. Henry packed his trunk again without a word.

He knew that his father's appointment was the result of Governor Seward's personal friendship; he did not then know that Senator Sumner had opposed it, or the reasons Sumner alleged for thinking it unfit; but he could have supplied proofs enough had Sumner asked, the strongest being that Mr. Adams had chosen a private secretary far more unfit than his chief. In the family history, its members had taken many a dangerous risk, but never before had they taken one so desperate.

Minister Adams sailed for England, May 1, 1861, with much the same outfit as Admiral Dupont would have enjoyed if the Government had sent him to attack Port Royal with one cabin-boy in a rowboat. Minister Adams remembered how his grandfather had sailed from Mount Wollaston in midwinter, 1778, on the little frigate Boston, taking his eleven-year-old son John Quincy with him, on a diplomacy of adventure that had hardly a parallel for success. He remembered too how John Quincy, in 1809, had sailed for Russia with himself, a baby of two years old, to cope with Napoleon and the Czar single-handed. He thought it natural that the Government should send him out as an adventurer also, with a twenty-three-year-old son, and he did not even notice that he left not a friend behind him.

Above all, the private secretary could not grumble to his chief. He never labored so hard to learn a language as he did to hold his tongue. He was already an adept when the party landed at Liverpool, May 13, 1861, and went instantly up to London: a family of early Christian martyrs about to be flung into an arena of lions, under the glad eyes of Tiberius Palmerston.

Then came the Trent Affair: the seizure of Mason and Slidell brought the Legation to the brink of war, and the Minister, summoned from Yorkshire, met the crisis without losing his nerve. The shock passed; the secretaries learned that patience, silence, and the closing of newspaper indiscretions were the only diplomacy left to them.
